title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial to test whether constrained prompting plus deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback (generate→verify→repair, one allowed repair) increases verifier-level semantic correctness when translating natural-language operator intents into low-level network configurations. Design: N=150 synthetic intents, shared_initial_candidate semantics, model=gpt-5-mini, deterministic validator=deterministic_netops_validator_v5, adapter family=hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Each intent produced one initial generation shared across baseline and guarded conditions; the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call. Results: baseline = 149/150 (99.333%); guarded = 150/150 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.006667 (≈0.67 pp); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Only one guarded repair was applied. Interpretation: on this preregistered synthetic corpus the guarded workflow produced a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement over a near-ceiling baseline. We emphasize the methodological lesson that pilot baseline calibration is necessary to avoid ceiling effects that invalidate preregistered power assumptions. All execution artifacts, configuration records, and analysis files are archived in the execution bundle referenced by the manifest.

sections.introduction:
Operational network engineering increasingly explores natural-language intent interfaces that translate human operator descriptions into executable low-level configurations. This translation task is attractive for reducing human burden and enabling intent-driven automation, but prior studies report frequent syntactic and semantic errors in single-pass LLM outputs that can produce unsafe or incomplete configurations requiring downstream correction. Deterministic verifier-guided generate→verify→repair pipelines are therefore a commonly proposed defensive architecture: models produce a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks the candidate against a formalized intent invariant, and an automated repair (or human gate) corrects violations before execution. Security analyses further motivate such gating because textual claims can be converted to real actions in tool-augmented agentic pipelines, producing claim-to-action vulnerabilities if unchecked.

Research question. After an autonomous literature review and preregistration we posed a tightly constrained confirmatory question: does constrained prompting (structured templates and semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase verifier-level semantic correctness of NL→configuration translation versus an unconstrained baseline under a paired design? The trial was preregistered (study_cand_2026_b2_v1) and frozen before observing model outputs.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifactized paired confirmatory trial measuring deterministic-verifier pass/fail as the primary endpoint on a synthetic intent corpus. (2) A complete execution and analysis package (N=150 paired items; completed episodes = 300; model calls used = 151) comparing baseline free-text prompting to constrained-template prompting plus at most one verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. (3) An empirical, artifact-grounded outcome: on this synthetic corpus the guarded pipeline produced a negligible numerical improvement (0.67 pp) over an already near-ceiling baseline; we draw methodological recommendations (pilot baseline calibration, explicit generation semantics, and repair-budget sensitivity) for future preregistered NetOps trials.
sections.related_work:
Work relevant to this study falls into three interlocking strands. First, intent-to-configuration research documents the difficulty of mapping free-text operator intents to verifier-sound formal artifacts and reports modest semantic-correctness rates on public benchmarks; these studies motivate formal verification or post-generation checks. Second, generator-plus-verifier and iterative repair architectures (generate→verify→repair) have been shown to improve correctness in infrastructure-as-code and configuration-repair tasks when paired with deterministic or policy-guided verifiers; reported gains depend strongly on baseline competence, repair budget, and sampling semantics. Third, security and systems analyses of agentic LLM pipelines demonstrate that unchecked model outputs can be transformed into harmful tool calls, motivating auditable gating and verifier-aware planning.

Our trial operationalizes a narrowly specified guarded architecture and places emphasis on preregistration, paired inference, and deterministic-verifier-level endpoints. Compared with prior work that reported larger guarded-vs-baseline gains, we differ in four crucial aspects that affect effect size: (a) shared_initial_candidate execution semantics (one initial sample shared across conditions), (b) a strict one-repair budget per intent, (c) a single tested model (gpt-5-mini), and (d) a synthetic verifier-capable task bank restricted to small topologies. These contrasts explain why observed marginal repair benefit here is smaller than some prior reports that used independent sampling or larger repair budgets.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory design. The study preregistration (study_cand_2026_b2_v1; preregistration SHA-256 = aea996afce45e3798345f6e32ae6c347456f103ecdb84fc36e27bb486a329399) defined a paired_binary design with primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The primary test was an exact two-sided McNemar with 95% bootstrap percentile CI computed from 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistration fixed N=150 confirmatory tasks to detect an absolute improvement of ≈15 percentage points with ≈80% power under conservative discordant-pair assumptions; the sampling plan, inclusion/exclusion rules, and analysis scripts were frozen prior to execution.

Task generation, families, and pre-filters. Confirmatory tasks were programmatically generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and cover four intent families: reachability/isolation patterns, ACL-like access changes, VLAN/MTU sequence changes, and uplink switchover patterns. Topology sizes were restricted to verifier-capable small networks (4–32 nodes). A rule-based ambiguity detector and parser/verifier-coverage checks were applied deterministically prior to model calls; no confirmatory exclusions occurred in this run (exclusions = 0). Each task manifest entry records generation_seed, required_sequence, and expected_final_state to allow deterministic replication of the synthetic corpus.

Model, adapter, and verifier. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (provider record: openai_responses). Adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 enforced per-task model-call budgets. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) implemented a full-intent-constraint validation rule returning a boolean pass/fail plus a normalized final-configuration text and validation diagnostics. Important runtime-reporting clarification required by review: the archived execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (unset). We therefore did not enforce a deterministic sampling temperature or fixed random-seed for the LLM; model outputs may be nondeterministic across independent API sessions. All per-call runtime sampling metadata and provider-call logs were archived.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and their inferential meaning. The execution contract used the shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initial model generation was produced and that identical sampled candidate was used to evaluate both baseline and guarded conditions. The guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call only if the deterministic verifier failed that initial candidate. Consequently, the observed baseline success rate measures the validity of that single initial sampled candidate; the guarded vs baseline contrast therefore isolates the marginal effect of the single allowed repair applied to the identical initial sample. This semantics constrains the estimand to marginal repair benefit rather than to differences that could arise from independent per-condition sampling.

Execution budget, retries, and missingness policy. The adapter enforced exactly one initial model call per intent and at most one repair call per intent (planned episodes = 300; maximum_model_calls = 300). Missingness and failure policies were preregistered: one deterministic retry on API timeout followed by marking as failed if persistent; the primary analysis used complete-pair exclusion and a prespecified sensitivity analysis treating missing guarded outputs as failures. During the run no episode failed or was excluded; complete_pair_count = 150 and missingness = 0.

Scoring and analysis. The deterministic validator applied a full_intent_constraint_validation rule; primary outcome is verifier-level semantic correctness (binary pass/fail). The primary analysis used an exact two-sided McNemar on the paired contingency table and computed 95% bootstrap percentile CIs with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729). Secondary contrasts and multiplicity corrections were preregistered but not used as confirmatory in this execution because the constrained-only condition B was not realized as a separate confirmatory branch under the adapter's shared_initial_candidate enforcement. All analysis code, paired_contingency_table.csv, and condition_summary.csv are archived and referenced in the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Planned paired episodes = 300; completed_episode_count = 300; complete_pair_count = 150; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations observed = 1. No episodes failed or were excluded; analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports zero missing or unscorable episodes. The deterministic_reconciliation.json artifact records provider_call auditing: hosted_model_call_event_count = 151, stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 150, repair = 1, and all deterministic consistency checks passed.

Primary numerical outcomes. Paired contingency counts (guarded × baseline): n_11 = 149 (both-pass), n_10 = 1 (guarded-only-pass), n_01 = 0 (baseline-only-pass), n_00 = 0 (both-fail). Per-condition success rates: baseline_success_count = 149/150 = 0.9933333333333333; guarded_success_count = 150/150 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00666666666666671 (≈0.67 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). The contingency table and per-condition summary are archived in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv respectively.

Repair diagnostics and revision iterations. Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150), consistent with the near-ceiling initial success rate; median revision iterations in guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). The single repair converted one initially invalid candidate to a valid configuration under the deterministic validator. The execution manifests include validator_trace records per episode showing validation_before and validation_after states, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes (empty for passed items), and normalized_configuration strings.

Representative artifact-grounded examples. Representative tasks illustrate typical intents and validator traces. Example (task-000001): intent — "Migrate edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600. For safety, shut edge1 down before changing either VLAN or MTU, then restore it to admin up." Shared-initial and both condition responses produced the expected four-command sequence; validator_trace.validation_after recorded normalized_configuration matching the reference, parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, and valid = true. Example artifacts (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt) and scorer outputs are archived and referenced by SHA-256 in the manifest.

Audit and contamination checks. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty (no contamination flags). Pre-execution unit-tests for mapping code and verifier-input transformations ran and passed; mapping failures or verifier 'unsupported-feature' responses would have triggered exclusion per the preregistered protocol but none occurred. Provider-call logs and per-call metadata confirm fresh isolated API sessions for each model call; cross-condition cache-key reuse was not observed.
sections.discussion:
Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch. The preregistered power analysis targeted detecting an absolute improvement of ≈15 percentage points with N=150, assuming a substantially lower baseline. Observed baseline initial-candidate success (149/150 ≈ 99.33%) left minimal room for improvement and produced a ceiling effect that rendered the planned confirmatory contrast uninformative. Practically, this outcome illustrates the necessity of a short pilot baseline-calibration step in preregistered NetOps trials to align task difficulty and sample size with the chosen model and prompts.

Interpretation constrained by shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because the same initial sampled candidate was used to evaluate both baseline and guarded conditions, the marginal effect attributable to the guarded pipeline is strictly the additional benefit from at most one repair applied to that identical candidate. This interpretation differs from designs that sample independently per condition or that permit multiple iterative repairs; those alternative semantics can produce larger observable differences and answer different estimands (e.g., end-to-end pipeline robustness averaged over independent draws).

Operational implications beyond the binary endpoint. Even when a guarded pipeline yields negligible numerical improvement under a single binary verifier pass/fail metric, guarded architectures have operational value not captured by that endpoint: they provide auditable decision records, deterministic verdicts for human approval gating, and standardized repair prompts that can feed operator dashboards. For production adoption, these non-statistical benefits may outweigh small numeric gains measured on synthetic corpora.

Relation to prior work and generality. Our artifact-grounded result does not contradict prior reports of larger guarded-vs-baseline gains in settings with lower baseline competence, independent sampling semantics, or richer repair channels. Instead, it bounds the marginal benefit of a one-repair guarded pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics with gpt-5-mini on a deterministic synthetic corpus and validator. Evaluating independent-sampling semantics, larger repair budgets, model diversity, or production-scale topologies remains necessary to generalize beyond this narrow empirical bound.

Design recommendations. Based on the preregistered artifacts we recommend: (1) a pilot phase to estimate baseline initial-candidate correctness for the selected model and prompts before fixing sample size; (2) explicitly stating generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate vs independent sampling) aligned with the estimand; (3) preregistering repair-budget sensitivity analyses (one vs multiple repairs) and reporting repair-stage invocation distributions; and (4) running and archiving validator-coverage unit-tests before model calls to avoid contamination by mapping or translator bugs.

Threats to validity. Internal: shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate marginal repair effect but do not measure inter-condition sampling variance. Construct: verifier pass/fail is a machine-checkable proxy for semantic correctness and depends on mapping code and validator coverage; mapping errors would bias outcomes (pre-execution unit-tests were executed and archived). External: single model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic tasks, and small topologies limit claims about production WANs and vendor CLIs. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions were invalidated by ceiling baseline behavior; exact McNemar p = 1.0 and bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02] quantify the limited inferential power to detect sizable improvements in this setting.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial comparing baseline free-text prompting to constrained-template prompting plus a single verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. On the archived synthetic corpus with gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator, the guarded pipeline increased verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (0.67 percentage points), a numerically tiny and statistically non-significant difference (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The principal scientific lesson is methodological: preregistered NetOps trials should include baseline calibration to avoid ceiling effects and preserve statistical power. Technically, our artifacts bound the marginal benefit of a single-repair guarded pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics; evaluating independent-sampling semantics, larger repair budgets, model diversity, and production-scale topologies remains important future work.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures deterministic validator pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
